props.text: In Animal Farm last weekend I read about Napoleon taking Jessie and Bluebell's nine puppies away to educate them himself, up in a loft where the other animals couldn't see them. I remember wondering why nobody asked what teaching them would involve. I was trying to stay open-minded about him, because organising things can look secretive from the outside.

I read some Animal Farm during the holiday and remember the sheep chanting four legs good, two legs bad when other animals might have had something to say. My notes just say 'noise ends discussion'. They don't say what the argument was about, and after several evenings of interrupted reading the meetings have blurred together.

In Chapter 5 (Chapter V), Squealer says, “Do not imagine, comrades, that leadership is a pleasure! On the
contrary, it is a deep and heavy responsibility.” He presents Napoleon’s taking on extra labour as a sacrifice and suggests the animals might make the wrong decisions if allowed to choose for themselves. Meanwhile, decisions about the farm move from Sunday meetings with debates to a private pig committee. Together, those claims frame the loss of a say as protection from the animals’ own mistakes, rather than as a loss of participation.

I can see why your project lead’s burden language might make questioning feel guilt-laden, especially after the planning meetings ended. Acknowledging someone’s workload and wanting a voice in a changed plan can both be valid. What feels hardest to question: the claim that they’re carrying the burden, or the decision being made without the planning meetings?
